chunks: Ali (peace be upon him) from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who takes the thief, whether he should present him to the Imam or leave him. He said: Indeed, Safwan ibn Umayya was lying in the Sacred Mosque, so he placed his cloak and went out to pour water. When he returned, he found his cloak had been stolen. He said: 'Whoever took my cloak?' and went looking for it, so he caught the thief and presented him to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Cut his hand.' Safwan said: 'You will cut his hand for the sake of my cloak, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then I forgive him for it.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him: 'Why did you not do this before you presented him to me?' I said: 'So the Imam is in the same position as the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) when presented to him?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'And I asked him about forgiveness before it reaches the Imam?' He said: 'It is good.'

key_terms.بِمَنْزِلَتِهِ: in the same position/status as him

ai.seo_question: Can the victim forgive the thief before the case reaches the Imam in Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfarayini elucidates the juristic distinction between the victim's right to forgive (afw) and the authority's right to enforce punishment (hudud) in theft cases. It highlights the principle that while the victim may waive their claim before the case is formally elevated to the Imam, once the matter is presented and evidence is established, the Imam assumes the authority to enforce the cutting of the hand, mirroring the Prophet's prerogative. This establishes the Imam's role as the successor in judicial authority, ensuring that personal forgiveness does not automatically nullify the public aspect of the crime once adjudication begins.
